title: A retry must find the first result
excerpt: Any request your app sends may be executed more than once, and nobody will know. Why a second charge ends customer trust, why the promise belongs to the business rather than the engineer, and the three places idempotency stops being simple.
detailTitle: A retry must find the first result
prose:
There is a fact about mobile networks that should be printed at the top of every requirements template. Any request your app sends may be executed more than once, and neither the user nor the app will know. Not sometimes, on purpose, during a migration. Routinely, as ordinary traffic, because timeouts lie.

The sequence is always the same and it takes about four seconds. The user taps pay. The request reaches your server and succeeds. The response dies somewhere on the way back, which the app cannot distinguish from the request having failed. The screen says failed. The user taps again. On a weak connection this is not a catastrophe to be handled later. It is Tuesday.

So somewhere in your system there is a customer who has been charged twice for one seat, or charged twice for one donation, or paid out twice for one survey. Your logs will show two successful payments. Your provider will show two successful payments. Every system you own will agree that this is correct, because from where each of them sits, it was.

The business is making this promise, not the engineer

Here is the part that gets argued about in the wrong room. A retry can never charge twice is not an implementation detail for an engineer to sort out later. It is a promise the business makes to its customers, and it belongs in the requirements document in the same words the customer would use, because it will eventually conflict with something else the business wants.

It will conflict. Almost always it conflicts with a nicer screen. The straightforward thing to do on a duplicate tap is to show an error, because an error is honest about the fact that something went wrong. The customer-friendly thing to do is show progress, and let the user keep tapping. If the promise is that a retry can never double-charge, then the progress screen wins and the error screen has to go, and somebody senior has to sign that trade-off rather than discovering it in production.

The same argument applies to a seat. Whether a second tap on the last seat shows a clear no or quietly fails, and whether the first payment is refunded immediately or after a support conversation, is a decision about how a bad day is handled in front of a customer. It is worth deciding in advance, while nobody is standing at a dock watching it.

What it actually costs to build

The guarantee itself is not expensive, and that is the part that surprises people. Three pieces, and none of them require a distributed system.

The identity of the operation. Every attempt carries a key generated once, on the device, before the first tap. A donation carries its intent identifier. A booking carries the key that produced it. That key is what lets the second tap be recognised as the same act rather than a new one, and it has to be created before the request goes out, because after the request there is no safe moment left.

The rule for repetition. When a key arrives that has already been used, the server returns the original outcome instead of doing the work again. A repeated donation returns the first donation, already recorded, with its receipt. A repeated seat booking returns the seat that was already held. This is a lookup before it is an insert, and it needs a database constraint underneath it, because an application-level check is a race condition with good manners.

The customer's view of a collision. What the screen says when the payment already succeeded, when the seat is already held by this same person, when the reward is already recorded. This is the part most often skipped, and skipping it produces something worse than a duplicate charge, which is a duplicate charge combined with an error message and a customer who now thinks your company has no idea what happened to their money.

The expensive work is not the transaction. It is deciding that the first press is the authoritative one and that the screen should say so calmly rather than apologising.

It is not only payments

The same guarantee protects anything that moves money, inventory, or a promise. I have needed it in situations that have nothing to do with a card.

A payment provider that delivers the same webhook twice, out of order, hours later, after you have already marked the transaction failed. A wallet payout where a mobile money transfer succeeds and the confirmation never comes back, so the user taps again and the row is inserted a second time. A row-level lock that deducts, holds a pending state, calls the provider, and compensates in a second transaction if the provider refuses, so that a double tap cannot produce two transfers. A reward where the user completes a survey and three separate signals report it, all of which converge on one payout rather than three.

In every case the mechanism is identical and the reasoning is identical. The operation has an identity, the identity resolves to one outcome, and the user is shown that outcome rather than a fresh attempt.

Where it gets uncomfortable

Idempotency is straightforward right up to the moment it intersects with something else, and I have learned most of what I know about it from the places it collides.

The first collision is refunds, because refunds are where retry logic goes to die. A refund request needs its own identity and its own status, a repeated refund request resolves to the same refund record rather than a second payment out, a partial refund has to be either supported or explicitly declared out of scope, and the refund has to change the state of the booking it belongs to. A refunded booking is not a confirmed booking with a footnote, and a support agent reading two screens should never have to guess which one is current.

The second collision is expiry. A key protects against repetition, but a hold has a clock, and a key that can be replayed forever is a key that can resurrect an expired hold. Somewhere the system has to decide whether a retry arriving after the hold died is a retry, which should return the original failure, or a new attempt, which should be treated as new. There is no universally correct answer and it depends on whether your customer would rather be told nothing happened or be sold the seat they were trying to buy.

The third is the failure nobody sees. Duplicate charges are reported immediately, because the customer is looking at their bank statement and they are angry. Duplicate payouts are reported later, sometimes after the money has been withdrawn. Duplicate donations are reported later still, because the donor has no reason to check twice. By the time the pattern is visible to you, it may have run for a month across every device on a bad connection, and you will see it as a strange cluster of complaints rather than as the retry pattern it actually is. That is worth logging for, deliberately, because the alternative is waiting to be told.

The question to ask your team

If your app moves money, holds inventory, or promises a reward, ask whoever built it what happens when the same person presses the same button twice on a bad connection. Not what is supposed to happen. What does happen.

If the answer is a description of the intended flow rather than a description of the code path, you have a promise on your website that your backend has not agreed to yet.

title: A hold must end by itself
excerpt: A hold with no expiry is not a booking, it is inventory loss. Why releasing a seat is a pricing decision with an owner's name on it, the three mechanisms that recover it, and why the expiry rate is really a measure of your checkout.
detailTitle: A hold must end by itself
prose:
Every booking system I have seen begin the same optimistic way. Someone taps a seat, the seat becomes theirs, and the implementation is reasonable because the requirement never asked what happens next. The tap happened. The seat is held. Everything the document described has occurred.

Then that person closes the app. Or their connection drops halfway through a card number, which on a weak signal is most of them. Or they get a call, or they simply change their mind. And the seat stays held, indefinitely, by a system that has no concept of a hold ending, because a hold that ends is a piece of business logic that nobody specified.

The consequence is not a bug. It is an empty bus, and an empty bus is invisible in every dashboard because the number in the database says the seat was sold.

The number that is not engineering

So somebody has to decide how long a hold lasts, and the decision will be made, and the most likely place for it to be made is in a configuration file by an engineer who picked a number that seemed reasonable. That number is a pricing decision. It is expressed in minutes, and it is one of the highest-leverage numbers in the entire product.

Too long and you sell inventory that does not exist. A seat held by an abandoned checkout at ten in the morning is still held at noon, still at closing, still tomorrow, and by then it is indistinguishable from a real booking in every report you run. You will conclude that demand fell, when what actually happened is that your own checkout flow consumed your inventory.

Too short and you break honest customers. Someone paying by card on a rural connection, or entering details for a relative, or using an authorisation their bank deliberately takes longer to approve, loses the seat they were buying while they were still in the middle of buying it. They will not blame the timeout. They will blame your product, and they will be right to.

Neither number is derivable from first principles. It depends on how your customers actually behave, how long your payment provider takes to answer, whether your market tends to book at the last minute, and what your competitors do. That is a business input, and it belongs in a document with the owner's name beside it, agreed before anybody builds the sweeper.

Three ways to release it, and why you need all three

Assuming the number exists, releasing a hold turns out to be three separate mechanisms, and in my experience projects that ship only one of them get support tickets about phantom bookings.

A scheduled sweep. This is the one that recovers inventory without anybody looking at it. A recurring job finds holds past their expiry and releases them. Without it, seats are only recovered when a customer happens to look at the same departure again, which means an evening rush can empty a bus and leave it empty until morning, and the morning rush finds nothing to sell.

A check at the moment of purchase. Before any seat is sold, confirm its hold has not already died. This is the guard that stops you overselling in the gap between the sweep running and the hold expiring, and it is the difference between the sweep being a clean-up and the sweep being load-bearing.

A notice to the person waiting. When a hold is released, the person who was holding it is somewhere between screens, possibly having walked away, possibly still typing. If they come back and the seat is gone with no explanation, they conclude the app is unreliable and they try somewhere else. This is the mechanism most often skipped, and it is the difference between losing a sale and losing a customer.

Why the duration is different in every business

The mechanics are identical in every product. The number is not, because the cost of being wrong is not.

A boat with a fixed number of seats absorbs failure publicly and immediately, in front of a person holding a ticket, at a dock, once. So it leans hard toward short holds and instant self-release, and it accepts that some honest customers lose a seat in exchange for never turning one away.

A bus network where each company settles its own day leans differently, because the failure mode is not a person at a dock, it is a company reconciling its books at closing and finding seats it cannot account for. That business needs the recovery to be complete and auditable, which pushes toward aggressive sweeping and toward recording every release with enough detail that the company can see where its inventory went.

A donation has no seats, but it has the same structure in a different currency. A donation in progress is held, it expires, and a donor who believes their donation went through must not be wrong about money. The bias there is the opposite. You would rather hold too long and risk a duplicate, which is visible and recoverable, than release too early and tell somebody their donation failed while their money moved.

Where my approach stopped working

On one product I made the hold duration configurable per company and let each one set its own number, on the reasonable theory that different operators think differently about pricing. In practice almost none of them ever changed it, and the ones that did set it far too long, which meant I had built a mechanism whose main effect was to give an owner a way to accidentally lose revenue while feeling that they had gained control.

What I do now is set a defensible default centrally, measure how many holds actually reach expiry in the first week, and bring that number back to the owner as evidence rather than as a question. A hold expiring at four percent probably means the duration is fine. A hold expiring at forty percent is a checkout that is failing in a way nobody is watching, and no duration setting fixes that, because the customer is leaving before they ever reach the payment step.

That distinction took me an embarrassingly long time to internalise. The expiry rate is not primarily a measure of the hold. It is a measure of the checkout, and treating it as a settings problem means tuning a number while the actual failure is somewhere earlier.

The question to ask your team

Ask what happens to a seat when the person holding it closes the app, and then ask who chose that number and where it is written down.

If the answer is that it is handled, and the number is in a config file with no name attached, then the release of that seat is currently being decided by a default that nobody chose, and your inventory is being spent on an opinion.

title: Clean it once on the way in
excerpt: Forgiving a misspelled city on every keystroke is cheaper to build and more expensive to keep. Why normalising names against a canonical list on the way in is the only approach that later lets you count, join, and report by place.
detailTitle: Clean it once on the way in
prose:
Every search that fails to find something should have returns an empty result, and an empty result is the most damaging thing a discovery product can show. It does not read as a mismatch. It reads as absence, and people conclude the thing they want does not exist here, which is a different conclusion from the one that is true.

The reason it happens so consistently is that it is not a query problem. The query is doing exactly what it was asked. The problem is upstream, in what was stored, and the two are easy to confuse because they produce the same symptom and live in different layers.

What the database is actually holding

Consider a city. In one product it arrives from a dropdown. In another it is typed by somebody whose keyboard produced a different character, or who speaks a second language and writes the name the way they say it, or who has moved between two spellings that are both correct in different places. In another it arrives through an integration written by somebody else years ago, before you were involved.

So the table accumulates Abidjan and Abidjan with a curved apostrophe and ABIDJAN and a spelling that is simply wrong, and none of them are bugs. Each was a real person making a reasonable attempt to type a real place. Now a person searches for the name they know, and the row holding their city does not match, and the list is empty, and they conclude your product has no results.

This is the failure I have seen most often in search, and it is the one where teams most reliably optimise the wrong thing, because the fix that feels productive is making matching more tolerant, which treats the symptom and adds cost to every query forever.

Two ways to fix the same problem

There are two ways to make an approximate name match an approximate stored name. Both work. They are not equivalent, and the difference is a permanent bill.

The first is to be forgiving at search time. Every keystroke goes to the database with a tolerant comparison, and it works, and it works for as long as the table is small. As it grows, tolerant comparison over free text stops using an index and starts reading the table. That is the moment search gets slow, and the moment the answer starts depending on how the database feels about your data that day rather than on what you asked for.

The second is to forgive once, at the moment the value enters the system. Keep a canonical list of places. When something arrives that is not on the list, match it tolerantly against that list, once, and store a reference to the canonical entry rather than the string somebody typed. After that, every search becomes an exact comparison against a reference, which is fast, indexable, and correct.

The second option has a cost people dislike, which is that it requires deciding what the canonical list is, and somebody has to own it. It also requires cleaning what already exists. Both are real costs. Both are one-time. The first option's cost is a permanently more expensive and permanently less predictable query, paid on every request forever, by every user, in exchange for never having to make the decision.

Why the second one wins even when it looks more work

The argument for forgiving at search time is that it never rejects a legitimate entry. That is true and it is exactly the trap, because it means the system has no way to say that two different things are the same place, and therefore no way to count, aggregate, price, or route anything by place.

Once place is a reference rather than a string, an ordinary evening of work becomes possible. You can show a user every result in the place they searched for, not only the ones whose spelling happened to match. You can join a booking against the same place a user searched, knowing they are the same place. You can report on inventory by city and get a number, instead of eleven numbers. None of that is a feature request. All of it falls out of having decided, once, what a place is.

I have done this in three different products for three different reasons, and in two of them I arrived at it late, after shipping the forgiving version and paying for it in slow queries and support questions about missing results. In the third I did it on the first day, and the only thing I had to do differently was write down the list before writing the form.

What it costs your team, honestly

Two things, and neither is technical.

Somebody has to own the list. Not write it once, own it. New places arrive, spellings change, a district is renamed, and somebody with the authority to add or retire an entry has to exist, or the list quietly becomes wrong and everything built on it becomes confidently incorrect. This is a small ongoing obligation and it is the reason this approach is often skipped, because it is invisible on a launch date.

And you have to decide what to do with data that arrives that does not match anything. Silently storing the unknown string is the default and it is how the table gets dirty in the first place. Rejecting it stops people using your product. The workable middle is to store it as unresolved, keep the product working, and surface the unresolved ones to whoever owns the list, so the debt is visible and someone is told. That is an operations habit, not a database feature, and it is the part that actually determines whether the list stays trustworthy.

Where my approach stopped working

Twice I have shipped the forgiving version and told myself the tolerance would be tightened later. Both times it was not tightened, because tightening it later is a data migration that breaks searching for real users, and nobody schedules that voluntarily.

What changed my habit was realising the decision is not really about search at all. It is about whether place, category, or skill is a thing your business can count. If it can only ever be a string, then nothing can be aggregated by it, reported by it, or joined against it, and your reporting will be approximate forever in a way nobody will be able to point at and explain.

So the question to ask is not how tolerant our matching should be. It is whether this value is an identifier in our business or a label on a string. Once that is answered, the engineering follows, and it follows the same way in every product I have worked on.

title: After the app is dead
excerpt: A message that only works while the app is open is not a notification. The dead-app case is the majority case in production, and the fallback that rescues a failed delivery is a budget line the owner has to sign before launch.
prose:
A crashed screen files a report. A failed payment files a ticket. An undelivered notification files nothing at all. Nothing throws, nothing logs, no alert fires, and the user simply does not come back. The retention curve sags for reasons nobody can name, and the team spends a fortnight rewriting the copy of messages that were never received.

The reason this failure is so consistently the most expensive one is that it is invisible from inside the product. Everything works. The code that sends the message succeeds, the provider accepts it, the logs show the right thing. The gap is between the moment the provider accepts a message and the moment a human being sees it, and almost no team has anything measuring that gap.

The only case worth designing for

Most notification work is built and tested with the app in the foreground, because that is the condition under which it is convenient to build and test. The message appears. The badge updates. The developer sees it work and the requirement is considered satisfied.

That is the easy case, and in production it is the minority case. The operating system decides when your app is alive and it is not generous about it. It suspends background work to save battery, terminates suspended apps to reclaim memory, restricts what runs in the background, throttles everything else, and does not tell your users when it has done any of it. On top of that, tokens expire, permissions get denied, users turn notifications off entirely, and manufacturers ship their own variations on the theme.

So the design question is not how to send a message. It is what happens when the message is sent and the device is not cooperating. That is not an edge case to be handled later. On any real product it is the majority of deliveries, and the user who needs a message is usually the one whose phone is least able to receive it.

The reminder that has to fire with no server

The clearest example I have worked on is a prayer reminder for communities where coverage is intermittent and phones are old. The requirement was one line long. People must receive reminders.

The only design that met it was to remove the server from the delivery path entirely. The schedule lives on the device. It is rebuilt from the underlying programme data every time the app launches, so it repairs itself whenever the app is opened rather than depending on a background job that may never run. It is rendered in the language of the programme rather than the language of the device, because the person receiving it and the person who set the device up are frequently not the same person.

Then the platform's own limits had to be respected rather than discovered. The system will only hold a limited number of scheduled notifications, so the plan is pruned to the nearest set across the weeks ahead, with enough lead time that the device has a chance to wake before the reminder is due. Permission is requested quietly, after the value has been demonstrated, because a prompt fired before anyone has seen a reminder is a prompt that gets permanently declined.

The result is a reminder that fires in airplane mode. It is not a clever fallback. It is the product working as designed, because the design assumed the worst case rather than treating it as a degraded path.

Where delivery quietly stops and nobody is told

Even when you have done all of that, delivery fails silently by default, and the three failure points are worth naming because each one needs its own handling.

The token is dead. Every push token has a finite life. It expires when the app is reinstalled, when the user resets the device, when the operating system revokes it, and eventually for no reason anybody can determine. A message sent to a dead token is accepted by the provider and delivered to nothing. If you are not checking, you cannot tell the difference between a message delivered and a message discarded, so tokens get pruned and the failures get logged, deliberately, because an unpruned dead token is a permanently broken recipient.

The permission is gone. The user denied it, or the system took it, or they simply switched notifications off for your app in settings. The message is accepted and never shown. There is no API that tells you this happened, which means the only way to find out is to measure whether anything came of the notification, and that requires knowing what came of it.

It arrived at the wrong moment. A departure warning that lands an hour after the bus has left is not a late message, it is misinformation, and it trains people to ignore the channel entirely. Timing is part of the contract, including quiet hours, the timezone the message is scheduled against rather than the one the device happens to be set to, and an expiry on the payload so the app can show something honest when the user finally opens it.

The message that costs money to rescue

Every one of those failures has an obvious remedy and the remedy is not free. Sending a text message instead costs money per message, and that turns the fallback into a budget decision, and a budget decision is not an engineering decision.

Which means somebody has to decide, per message class, whether it is worth a fallback at all, and sign it. A booking confirmation is worth it, because the customer has a plane to catch and the alternative is a stranded stranger. Marketing is not, because the speculative value of a message about something the customer did not ask for does not justify a per-message cost applied to a whole audience. And a one-time code is worth paying for, in the opposite direction, because the person cannot proceed without it.

In practice this is where notification projects quietly lose their budget, because the price of the fallback is discovered after launch, on an invoice, rather than being an amount the owner agreed to before the feature shipped. By then the fallback is load-bearing and cannot be turned off without losing the messages.

How you know it worked

The last piece is measurement, and most products skip it because the provider gives you a success response that does not mean what people assume it means. Accepted is not delivered. Delivered is not opened. Opened is not read.

What you can measure honestly is narrower and more useful. You can track, per message, whether anything came of it, in whatever way your product allows. A ticket opened shortly after a departure message. A login after a code. An action after a payment notice. That correlation is imperfect and it is still the only honest answer to the question the founder is actually asking, which is whether the person found out.

The test I use is simple and it is not a technical test. Pick the message in your product that matters most if it never arrives, and ask what your product does when it does not. If the honest answer is nothing happens and nothing is recorded, then your notification system is decorative, and the retention curve you are trying to explain has already been explained.

title: The feature is not the product. The business is.
excerpt: Search, booking, payment, identity, and messages are not features. They are decisions, and the right shape of each is set by what being wrong costs in your specific business. Why reusing last quarter's solution is how features ship broken.
detailTitle: The feature is not the product. The business is.
prose:
The most expensive thing I see in mobile development is a solution reused. Not stolen, not copied badly, reused by someone who genuinely believes it worked well somewhere else. It did work well somewhere else. That somewhere else had a different customer, a different failure, and a different definition of expensive. Reuse transfers all of that without telling you.

This is not a technology argument. It is a business one. Search, booking, payment, identity, and messages are not features. They are decisions, and the right shape of each decision is set by what being wrong costs in your specific business. The owner of that business is the only person who knows that number, and nobody asks them before the screens get drawn.

Search fails three ways, and businesses feel them differently

Every search I have worked on broke in one of three places. Something that should match did not, the wrong thing ranked first, or the right thing arrived too late. The diagnosis is identical across products. What differs is which of the three actually costs you.

A devotional library serving villages on a weak connection feels the third one hardest. A result that takes eight seconds is a result the person never sees, because they have walked away. A bus network booking across dozens of separate companies feels the second one, where the wrong trip appears first and a passenger commits to the wrong day. A rewards platform showing campaigns to people who are not eligible, or who have already been paid from an exhausted budget, feels the first, and it costs you money rather than patience.

Same three sentences. Completely different engineering priorities, and the priority is a business fact, not a technical one.

Booking leans toward whoever absorbs the failure

The mechanics of a reservation are largely settled. Hold the inventory, verify the payment, write the ticket together with the decrement, let the hold expire on its own, and make a repeated press return the first result. I have implemented exactly this shape for boats, for buses, for donations, and for surveys, and the reliability gain has been identical every time.

What changes is where the rules lean. A river boat with a fixed number of seats absorbs failure in public, at a dock, in front of a person holding a ticket. So it leans hard toward safety, short holds, and immediate self-release. A bus network where each company settles its own day absorbs failure in its accounts, so it leans toward separation, and one company's rush must never touch another company's numbers. A donation leans toward a single provable outcome, because a person charged twice for a donation does not retry. They leave, and they tell other people.

Payment is trust, and trust has different shapes

For payment the non-negotiable is the same everywhere. Verify on the server, never trust the device, and let a repeated press find the first result rather than creating a second charge. Every product I have shipped with money in it enforces this.

Beyond that, the trust object differs. For a donor it is the receipt, which has to arrive, has to be readable later, and sometimes has to survive a human reviewing a bank transfer. For a passenger booking from a dock with no account, it is a bill that matches exactly on both sides, down to rounding, because a mismatch means either an argument or a loss. For a platform settling dozens of independent companies, it is the separation of the books. For a rewards product, it is the wallet showing a real stored number rather than a hopeful one.

Identity depends on who the person actually is

People who travel without email need a phone number that survives reinstalls, because that number is the only thing tying them to their booking. People who arrive through a social sign-in need their profile, their chat identity, and their preferences created in one pass, or the product has a half-registered stranger in it. A company running drivers, cashiers, inspectors, and managers needs access separated by company and by responsibility, and revocation that actually takes effect rather than merely logging someone out of one device.

The same login screen solves none of these by itself. Which one you have is decided by who your customer is and what they have on them.

Messages are priced by what they are for

Every notification needs a channel order and a fallback, and the order follows the message's job. A habit has to arrive with no connection at all, which means the schedule lives on the device. A warning about a departure has to arrive on time, because an hour-late warning is misinformation. A payment needs its proof attached. A social action needs to restart a loop.

The expensive one is the fallback, because every fallback message costs money per send. Whether a confirmation is worth a text fallback, and whether marketing is, is a budget decision with your name on it. It should be signed before launch, not discovered on the first invoice.

The one question that prevents most of this

Before I design any of these, I ask the owner one question: what does being wrong cost you here? Not what should we build. What does the failure actually look like for your business, and who absorbs it.

If the answer is a passenger turned away at a dock, everything follows. If it is a person quietly gone after one failed message, everything follows. If it is a support morning, everything follows. The engineering is downstream of that answer, and that answer is not mine to invent. It is not even mine to guess at. It is the one thing I am obliged to ask for before drawing anything.

The owners I work best with are not the ones who know the answer immediately. They are the ones willing to sit with the question, because they understand that a feature built on a guessed answer will work perfectly and still be wrong for their business.

title: Requirements are a system, not a document
excerpt: Every failed mobile project I have been called into had a requirements document. It was reviewed, signed, and described every screen in careful detail. Then money went missing, seats sold twice, and notifications never arrived. The screens were correct. The system was not.
detailTitle: Requirements are a system, not a document
prose:
Every failed mobile project I have been called into had a requirements document. That is the uncomfortable part. The document existed, it was reviewed, it was signed. It described every screen, every button, every happy path in careful detail. And then the product shipped, and money went missing, and seats got sold twice, and notifications never arrived, and nobody could explain why — because the failure never lived on a screen. It lived between screens, in the gaps the document never specified: the retry that fired twice, the payment that succeeded while the app showed failure, the booking that expired while the user was still typing their card number. The screens were correct. The system was not.

This is the central lesson of business analysis for mobile products. On the web, a requirements document can get away with describing pages and clicks, because the environment is forgiving: the connection is usually present, the session is usually alive, the server is one hop away and holds all the state. On a phone, none of that is true. The device is offline half the time, the operating system kills your app without asking, the clock cannot be trusted, the user denies the permission your flow depends on, and every request you send may arrive zero, one, or five times. A requirements document that does not specify behavior under those conditions is not a specification. It is a wish. And wishes do not survive contact with the operating system.

So business analysis for mobile is not a paperwork discipline. It is an engineering discipline done in words before it is done in code. The analyst's job is to force every stakeholder conversation through the hostile reality of the device until the requirements describe a system that can actually exist on a phone — with states, transitions, timeouts, retries, conflicts, and acceptance criteria that mention airplane mode. This post is how I do that: the questions I ask, the artifacts I demand, and the places where mobile requirements most often lie by omission.

The phone is a hostile environment. Say so in writing.

Start here, because everything else follows. A serious mobile requirements process opens by writing down the environment the software will actually run in, and refusing to let anyone pretend it is a desk with fiber internet. My environment statement for a typical consumer product reads something like this: the app will run on low-end Android devices with 2GB of RAM; on networks that drop for minutes at a time; with users who deny notification and location permissions; with device clocks wrong by hours; with the OS killing the app in the background to save battery; with users on OS versions five years old. Every line of that statement is a requirement in disguise, because each one deletes an assumption the happy path was built on.

Consider what each environmental fact demands. Intermittent connectivity demands that every mutating operation specify its offline behavior: does the booking queue locally and sync later, like offline ticket sales across 30+ cities that must reconcile per tenant without double-selling? Or does it refuse and say so, like a payment that must never complete without server verification? There is no default answer. "It should just work" is not a requirement; it is the absence of one, and whichever behavior the engineer guesses will be wrong for half your users. I built donation flows for villages with poor networks where the entire design centered on this question, and collaboration features for musicians where it did not matter at all — same company skill set, opposite requirements, and only the environment statement told us which was which.

OS kills demand that no critical state live only in memory. If the app is murdered mid-checkout — and on Android, it will be — what does the user return to? A lost cart, a resumed flow, a completed booking they never saw confirmed? Permissions denied demand fallback paths specified per permission: no location means manual city entry with normalized names, not a crash and not a blank screen. Wrong clocks demand that every time-sensitive rule name its time authority, which is always the server, never the device. Old OS versions demand a floor: which versions you support is a business decision with support-ticket consequences, and it belongs in the requirements, not in a bug report six months later. None of this is engineering trivia. Each item is a business decision about what the product promises, and if analysis does not extract the promise, engineering cannot keep it.

Specify state machines, not screens

Stakeholders think in screens. Systems think in states. The single highest-leverage move in mobile business analysis is translating every feature from a sequence of screens into a state machine before a single UI requirement is written. Take booking, the feature I have rebuilt most often. The screen version goes: search trips, pick a seat, enter details, pay, see confirmation. The state version goes: a seat is free, held, paid, confirmed, expired, or released — and the entire product is the set of transitions between those states, who is allowed to trigger each one, how long each one lasts, and what happens when two people trigger conflicting transitions at the same moment.

Why does this matter? Because screens hide the decisions and states expose them. The screen flow never asks who releases a held seat when payment fails. The state machine cannot avoid the question: the held state needs a timeout, the timeout needs a duration, the expiry needs an actor (a scheduled job, checked on read, or both), and the release needs to notify the waiting user or not — each a business decision with revenue attached. A hold that never expires is inventory permanently stuck; I have seen boats and buses lose real sales to exactly this, seats locked by abandoned checkouts that no requirement ever released. A hold that expires too fast abandons legitimate buyers mid-typing. The duration of a seat hold is not a technical detail. It is pricing, conversion, and customer anger expressed as a number of minutes, and analysis must put that number in the document with the stakeholder's signature next to it.

Conflicts are the same story. Two users tapping the last seat within the same second is not an edge case on a popular route; it is Tuesday. The requirement must state the resolution: first verified payment wins, the loser gets an instant refund and an apology screen, and the apology screen is itself a specified state, not an error toast someone invents during QA. Double-sell prevention, waiting lists, overbooking policy — these are business rules wearing engineering clothes. My rule for any analyst I work with: if a feature involves inventory, money, or capacity, the requirements contain a state diagram with every transition labeled, or the requirements are not finished. Screens come after, and they come easily, because a screen is just one state's clothing.

Every tap will be retried. Write that down.

Here is a fact about mobile networks that should be printed at the top of every requirements template: any request the app sends may be executed more than once, and neither the user nor the app will know. Timeouts lie. The user taps pay, the request reaches the server, the response dies on the way back, the app shows failure, the user taps again. Without explicit design, you have just charged them twice. This is not a rare catastrophe; on flaky networks it is routine traffic. So idempotency — the property that repeating an operation has the same effect as doing it once — is not an implementation detail for engineers to sort out later. It is a business requirement, because "a retry can never double-charge" is a promise the business makes to its customers, and the document must contain it verbatim.

What does that look like in practice? For every operation that moves money, inventory, or points, the requirements state three things. First, the identity of the operation: each user intent carries a unique key (an idempotency key, a client-generated transaction reference), so that five arrivals of the same tap resolve to one outcome. Second, the resolution rule: a repeated key returns the original result instead of performing the operation again — the second tap shows "already paid," never a second charge. Third, the user-visible behavior for each collision: what the screen says when the payment already succeeded, when the seat is already held by this same user, when the donation already recorded. I have applied this pattern to bus ticketing across dozens of cities, to boat bookings with fixed capacity, to multi-gateway payments with per-company accounting, and to donation receipts a donor must be able to trust. The domains differ. The requirement is identical, and it belongs in analysis, because only analysis can get the business to confirm that "never double-charge" outranks "never show a confusing message" when the two conflict — and they will conflict.

Refunds deserve the same treatment, because refunds are where retry logic goes to die. The requirement must state: refund requests are tracked by status, a retried refund resolves to the same refund record, partial refunds are either supported or explicitly out of scope, and every refund changes the booking state it belongs to — a refunded booking is not a confirmed booking with a footnote. Webhook-driven status (the payment provider telling you what actually happened, asynchronously, possibly twice, possibly out of order) must be named as the source of truth, with the app's optimistic display explicitly labeled as provisional. Donors, riders, and finance teams all read different screens; the requirements must state the one truth those screens share and which system owns it. If your document says "integrate the payment gateway" and stops, you have specified a logo, not a payment system.

Time is a business rule. Name its authority.

Nearly every mobile product runs on time, and nearly every requirements document treats time as decoration. Holds expire. Prices change at midnight. Trips depart. Promo codes die. Sessions time out. And every one of these is a small contract with the user that the product will either honor exactly or break visibly. The analysis failure I see most often is specifying durations without specifying clocks: "the hold lasts 10 minutes" — ten minutes according to whom? The device clock, which the user can change, which drifts, which sits in the wrong timezone? Or the server clock, which requires a round trip the offline user cannot make? A hold that expires by device time can be extended forever by toggling the clock. A hold that expires by server time needs a sync strategy for the offline buyer. Both are buildable. Neither is the default. The document must choose.

Then comes expiry behavior, the most skipped paragraph in mobile requirements. Every timeout needs four specified answers: what triggers the check (a scheduled sweeper, lazy evaluation on next read, a push from the server), what state the object moves to (held becomes released, never deleted — the audit trail is a business asset), what the user is told (a notification, an in-app banner on next open, silence), and what happens to the money (auto-refund initiated, refund status tracked, receipt issued). An expired booking that keeps the user's money is not a timeout; it is theft with a timer. An expired hold that silently releases while the user stares at a pay button is a support ticket with a timer. I specify expiry as carefully as purchase, because from the user's perspective expiry IS the product in the failure case — it is the only part of the timeout they will ever experience, and it had better feel designed.

Timezones and calendars are the quiet killers. A trip departing at 8 PM in one city and booked from another, a donation receipt dated for tax purposes, a program schedule spanning regions — each needs the document to state the canonical timezone (usually the event's local time, stored as UTC, displayed per device locale) and the display rule. Daylight-saving transitions will move your 2:30 AM trip into nonexistence once a year; that is a requirement to find in analysis, not a bug to find in production. My standing rule: any feature where a human makes plans around a clock gets a time section in the requirements with authority, canonical storage, display rule, and expiry behavior. It takes one page. It prevents the class of bug that makes users miss boats.

Identity is a requirement, not a login screen

Documents love login screens. They show the phone-number field, the OTP boxes, the cheerful success state, and they stop — as if identity were a door you pass through once. On mobile, identity is the foundation every other feature stands on, and the requirements must treat it as infrastructure: who the user is, how the app knows across reinstalls and devices, what each role may touch, and how access dies. Get this wrong and you do not have an auth bug; you have a business where drivers see the wrong company's trips, where refunded users keep premium access, where a stolen phone keeps spending.

The first analysis question is what identity even means for this product. For a ride-hailing driver app, the phone number is the identity — it survives reinstalls, it matches the dispatch records, it works for users who have never owned an email address. For a two-sided marketplace, registration must provision half a dozen things at once: the profile, the chat identity, the notification tokens, the initial skills or preferences — and the requirements must state the atomicity: if step four of six fails, is the user registered or not? I have built both, and the document that says "user signs up with phone OTP" without specifying provisioning order, partial-failure behavior, and what the support agent sees, has specified a demo, not a system. Guest checkout sharpens the point further: a booking made without an account still needs an owner for refunds, receipts, and disputes, so the requirements must define the guest identity (phone number plus booking reference, say) and its upgrade path when the guest later registers. Every guest is a future support ticket; specify them now.

Roles and revocation close the loop. Hierarchical roles — platform admin, company admin, staff, driver, customer — each with explicit data boundaries: a company admin sees their own trips, never the neighbor company's; a staff member refunds but never reconfigures payouts. The requirements state the matrix, because "admin can manage bookings" will be interpreted five ways by five engineers. And revocation must be specified as a first-class flow, not assumed: when a driver is deactivated, do their active sessions die immediately or at next check? Are their tokens revoked server-side or merely deleted from the device (which the thief still holds)? Does the dashboard show the kill switch and its audit log? Access that cannot be revoked on demand is not access control; it is hope with a password field. Analysis writes the revocation requirement. Engineering builds the middleware. The founder sleeps.

Notifications are a delivery contract, not a feature

"The app should send push notifications" is the most expensive sentence in mobile requirements, because it reads as one feature and hides six. A serious notification requirement specifies the contract: which events notify, through which channels, with what fallback, linking where, counted how, and what happens when delivery fails. Miss any clause and the OS will fill it in — with silence. The failure is uniquely cruel: nothing crashes, no ticket is filed, the user simply never comes back, and the team debates message copy for messages that were never received. The copy was never the problem. The pipe was.

Channel strategy comes first. Push is the primary channel but the least reliable one: tokens expire, users disable permissions, manufacturers kill background services, iOS caps local scheduled notifications (I have built around the 60-item ceiling by rebuilding six-week reminder plans from program schedules, and the requirement had to state the horizon, the lead time, and the rebuild triggers — none of which appear in "send reminders"). So the requirements name the fallback per message class: booking confirmations fall back to SMS when push cannot deliver; marketing never does; OTP codes use SMS first with push as backup. Each fallback has a cost — per-message SMS pricing is a business number — so channel priority is a budget decision disguised as a technical one, and analysis must surface the price tag before launch, not after the first invoice.

Then the payload contract: every notification names its deep-link target (the exact chat, the exact booking, the exact trip — "opens the app" is a failed requirement), its badge semantics (whose unread count, synced from where, cleared by what action), its timing rules (quiet hours, timezone of delivery, expiry — a "your bus leaves in 10 minutes" delivered an hour late is misinformation), and its failure handling (dead tokens pruned and logged, ticket statuses tracked, undeliverable critical messages escalated to SMS). Dual-channel delivery — push plus email, or push plus in-app inbox — must state the dedup rule so the user is informed once, not spammed thrice. I specify notifications the way lawyers specify SLAs: event, channel order, fallback, target, timing, and proof of delivery. Because that is what they are. The retention curve your investors will stare at is built out of these clauses.

"Good search" must be measurable, or it is not specified

Search requirements are where business language goes vaguest — "fast, relevant search" — and where vagueness costs most, because search is the front door of discovery products and users judge it in one try. Serious search requirements decompose into three measurable promises: matching (nothing that should match is missing), ranking (the right things come first), and latency (results arrive before patience expires). Each gets numbers. Matching gets a test corpus: these fifty queries must return these items, including misspellings, French and English variants across African markets, inconsistent location names normalized to canonical cities. Ranking gets rules: proximity weighted against rating how? New listings boosted for how long? Paid placement labeled and separated from organic — a business decision with legal consequences, stated in analysis, not discovered in an app-store review. Latency gets a budget: first results in under 400 milliseconds on a mid-range device on 3G, with the payload sizes and index strategy that budget implies.

The mobile-specific clauses matter most. Search must specify its offline behavior (cached recent searches? a browsable subset? an honest empty state?), its per-keystroke cost (debounced queries against a local index versus server round trips that burn data plans), and its empty and failed states as designed screens with specified copy and next actions — because "no results" is the moment the user decides whether your product understands them, and a blank page is a decision too. Filters are business rules: which facets exist, which combinations are valid, what "near me" means in kilometers per market. I have built discovery across musician skills with proximity ranking, campaign matching across employment and eligibility attributes, and city-route-station lookup across dozens of tenant-isolated cities. Every one of them reduced, after the first month of complaints, to one of three sentences: something is missing, the order is wrong, or it is too slow. Requirements that name all three sentences before launch get few complaints after it.

Acceptance criteria that survive the operating system

All of the above converges on one artifact: acceptance criteria written for the device that exists, not the demo that flatters. The standard Given-When-Then format works — provided the givens are allowed to be hostile. "Given the user is on the payment screen" is a weak given. "Given the user is on the payment screen with airplane mode on," "given the app was killed after the payment request was sent," "given the user double-taps the pay button," "given the session expired while the form was open" — these are the givens that separate specified software from hopeful software. My rule: every story that moves money, inventory, or identity carries at least one hostile given, or it goes back to analysis.

Concrete examples, from real documents. Booking: "Given a seat is held with 3 minutes remaining, when the payment succeeds at minute 4, then the booking is confirmed only if the hold is still valid; otherwise the payment is auto-refunded, the seat is released, and the user sees the seat-unavailable screen with alternative trips." That single criterion forced decisions about hold duration, expiry checks, refund initiation, and the apology screen — four business decisions hiding inside one user story. Notifications: "Given the device token is stale, when a booking confirmation is triggered, then the system sends SMS within 60 seconds and logs the push failure; the user receives exactly one message." That criterion forced channel priority, fallback timing, dedup, and observability. Authentication: "Given the user reinstalls the app, when they verify the same phone number, then their bookings, receipts, and notification preferences are restored without contacting support." That criterion forced the identity model, the guest-upgrade path, and the backup strategy. Each criterion is a paragraph. Each paragraph prevented a class of production incident. This is the highest-ROI writing in the entire project, and it happens before a line of code.

Non-functional criteria need the same hostility. Performance: "search returns first results within 400ms on the reference low-end device on throttled 3G" — with the reference device named, because "fast on my flagship" is how latency budgets die. Reliability: "no confirmed booking is ever lost across app kill, reinstall, or 24 hours offline; the booking is visible on next launch after sync." Security: "a revoked driver token is rejected within 60 seconds; deactivation from the dashboard propagates without requiring app update." Usability under constraints: "every critical flow completes with notification permission denied, location denied, and dark mode on." Read that last one again — it costs nothing to write and catches an entire category of assumption. The QA team will bless you. More importantly, the users on $80 phones in low-signal villages — the users most products claim to serve and fewest specify for — will actually be able to use what you built.

Why mobile estimates explode, and how analysis defuses them

Founders ask why the estimate doubled between the proposal and the plan. The honest answer is the state matrix: the requirements described one path, and engineering priced the matrix. Every feature on mobile multiplies across devices (flagship to five-year-old budget phones), OS versions (each with different permission models, background limits, and quirks), network conditions (online, offline, flapping, captive portals), permission states (granted, denied, denied-forever, revoked mid-flow), and app states (foreground, background, killed, Russiagate — I mean, updated mid-session). Nobody builds the full cross product. But the estimate must account for deciding, per feature, which cells are supported, which degrade, and which are explicitly out of scope — and that decision work is business analysis, not engineering padding.

The scoping tool I use is the explicit non-goal. For each feature, the document states what it will not do, with the stakeholder's initials: no offline ticket sales in phase one (with the revenue implication stated); no partial refunds (with the support-script implication stated); no support below Android 10 (with the excluded-user percentage stated). Non-goals convert silent assumptions into priced decisions, and they are where estimates shrink without quality shrinking — because half the matrix was never business-critical, it was just unspecified, and unspecified work gets built anxiously and tested never. The other estimator's friend is the boring-states inventory: for every screen, the requirements name its loading, empty, error, offline, and permission-denied states, or mark them inherited from a shared pattern. Five states times twenty screens is a hundred small designs; unlisted, they surface during QA as a hundred arguments. Listed, they take an afternoon. This is what "analysis reduces cost" actually means in practice: not cheaper hours, but fewer surprises, and surprises are the most expensive line item in any mobile budget.

The one-page checklist

If this post had to compress into the single page I tape to the wall at project kickoff, it would be these questions, answered in writing before design starts. What is the environment — devices, networks, OS floor, permissions reality? What are the states of every inventory, money, and capacity object, with all transitions, actors, and timeouts labeled? Which operations are idempotent, what carries the operation identity, and what does the user see on collision? Where does time come from, what expires, who checks expiry, and what happens to the money and the message when it does? What is identity — including guests, roles, provisioning atomicity, and revocation latency? What is the notification contract — events, channel order, fallback costs, deep-link targets, badge rules, quiet hours? What are the search numbers — matching corpus, ranking rules, latency budget on a named reference device? Which acceptance criteria carry hostile givens — airplane mode, killed app, double-tap, expired session? And what is explicitly out of scope, with the business cost of each exclusion stated? Nine questions. Answer them, and the document describes a system. Skip them, and it describes a demo — and demos, as every founder learns exactly once, do not process payments.

The deeper point is about who business analysis serves. It does not serve process; it serves the user holding a cheap phone in a dead zone with money at stake, and the founder whose business must be correct for that user on the first try — because on mobile there is rarely a second try. The app that double-charges is deleted. The ticket that never arrives is bought elsewhere next time. The notification that never lands is a customer quietly gone. Requirements are where those outcomes are decided, months before code, in plain sentences, by people willing to ask hostile questions of friendly screens. Write them like an engineer. Sign them like a founder. The operating system will test them either way.
